text: This lesson covers two tools built to work together: find, which locates files matching criteria like name, type, size, or age, and xargs, which takes a list of results and runs a command against every single one of them, without you writing a loop.

find walks a directory tree and matches files against the criteria you give it. Searching by name with a wildcard pattern finds every log file under /var/log on a Northbridge Retail server, while adding -type d instead narrows that same search down to directories only, like catching a stray node_modules folder.

find also filters by size and by modification time. -size plus a number and a unit finds files over a given size, which is exactly how you'd spot an access log that's quietly grown past 100 megabytes. And -mtime plus a number finds files older than that many days, useful for locating stale temp files nobody's touched in a month.

The -exec flag runs a command directly on every matching file, with curly braces standing in for the current file and a literal semicolon ending the command. That's how Northbridge's ops team deletes application logs older than ninety days in a single find command, with no loop written at all.

xargs takes lines of input — often piped straight from find — and builds them into arguments for another command. It's generally faster than -exec on large result sets, and it's the only real option when the command you're running needs its argument somewhere other than the end, which is exactly what xargs with a placeholder flag gives you.

find locates exactly the files you mean, and -exec or xargs acts on all of them at once instead of one by one. Up next, lesson seventeen: environment variables and PATH, which decide where the shell goes looking for the very commands you've been running all along.
